nameStory: The King Eider earns its royal name from the male's spectacular breeding plumage, featuring a crown of orange and yellow that makes him look like he's wearing a jeweled crown. Among all the eiders, this species was considered the most magnificent and regal-looking, truly the 'king' of its family.
description: The King Eider is a large, stocky sea duck that spends most of its time in cold ocean waters. Males in breeding plumage are absolutely stunning with bright orange crowns, blue-gray heads, and black and white bodies, while females and non-breeding males are mottled brown for camouflage. These hardy ducks are built for life in frigid Arctic and sub-Arctic waters, with dense, insulating feathers that keep them warm in conditions that would challenge most other waterfowl. They're substantial birds, noticeably larger and more robust than typical ducks you'd see on a pond.

idTips.label: Male's orange crown
idTips.description: Breeding males sport a distinctive puffy orange and yellow knob above their bill that looks like a colorful crown - this bright ornament is unmistakable and catches sunlight beautifully

idTips.label: Stocky sea duck build
idTips.description: Much more robust and heavy-bodied than typical ducks, with a thick neck and broad chest that gives them a powerful, chunky appearance on the water

idTips.label: Male's blue-gray head
idTips.description: Breeding males have soft powder-blue to gray coloring on their head and neck that contrasts beautifully with the bright orange crown

idTips.label: Female's mottled brown plumage
idTips.description: Females and young males are covered in rich, warm brown feathers with darker barring that creates a complex mottled pattern perfect for blending into rocky shorelines

idTips.label: Ocean habitat preference
idTips.description: Almost always seen in saltwater environments, riding the swells with ease and diving beneath the surface to feed on marine creatures

habitat: In New England, King Eiders are found exclusively in coastal marine waters, particularly during winter months when they move south from their Arctic breeding grounds. Look for them in deeper offshore waters, rocky coasts, and areas with strong currents where they can dive for sea urchins, mollusks, and crustaceans. They prefer the cold, nutrient-rich waters off Maine's coast and occasionally venture into Massachusetts waters during harsh winters.

seasonality.spring: Some individuals may still be present in early spring before migrating north to Arctic breeding grounds. Males beginning to show their spectacular breeding plumage.
seasonality.summer: Rarely seen in New England during summer as they migrate to Arctic tundra to breed and raise young in the far north.
seasonality.fall: First arrivals from the north begin appearing in late fall, with numbers building as winter approaches and Arctic waters freeze.
seasonality.winter: Peak time for King Eider sightings in New England waters, when they retreat south from ice-covered Arctic seas. Males may show full breeding plumage by late winter.

funFact: King Eiders can dive down to 180 feet underwater - deeper than a 15-story building is tall - and hold their breath for up to 4 minutes while hunting for sea urchins and shellfish on the ocean floor, making them some of the most accomplished diving athletes in the bird world.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Common Eiders, but male King Eiders have that distinctive bright orange crown knob while Common Eider males have black caps and white backs. Memory trick: 'King wears a crown' - look for that orange bulge above the bill.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'King' Eiders, these birds spend most of their lives as humble ocean nomads, only the breeding males display the royal plumage that gives them their majestic name. The rest of the year, and all females, look quite modest and practical for their harsh marine lifestyle.
compareHints: King Eiders are much more colorful than their Common Eider relatives, especially the males with their bright orange facial ornaments versus the Common Eider's simpler black and white pattern. King Eiders also prefer deeper, more offshore waters while Common Eiders often stay closer to shore and rocky intertidal areas. Both species are large sea ducks, but Kings have a more compact, rounded appearance.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common Eiders are much more abundant than their relative the King Eider in New England waters.
